Notes: The study develops a Sinhala OCR system integrated into an open-source word processor; it does not examine the OSS project’s lifecycle, maintenance, or sustainability.

Author: S. Huda; M. B. Musthafa; Y. Nogami
Title: Zeek Intrusion Detection on Raspberry Pi for IoT-Based Agriculture Monitoring Systems: Preliminary Investigation
Abstract Note: The increasing adoption of IoT technologies in agriculture has transformed crop monitoring and management practices. However, as agricultural networks become increasingly connected, they also become potential targets for cyber threats. These threats pose significant risks to the security and integrity of farming operations. Our previous work focused on developing an IoT application for plant agriculture monitoring systems that incorporated power management techniques and secure authentication mechanisms. To further enhance the security of that system, there is a need for intrusion detection capabilities to identify and mitigate evolving cyber threats in the network. This paper presents a preliminary investigation of implementing Zeek, an open-source intrusion detection system (IDS), to secure IoT devices in agricultural scenarios. We deploy Zeek in a Raspberry Pi virtual environment using VirtualBox, as it provides a controlled and isolated testing environment. Then, we evaluate the performance and capability of Zeek in detecting intrusions using a pcap file containing a mix of genuine and malicious traffic from Stratosphere laboratory dataset. We analyze multiple cyber threats relevant to IoT agriculture, including unauthorized access attempts and distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. We confirm the effectiveness of Zeek's performance based on the number of detected attacks, detection times and resource utilizations. Zeek uses 28.3% of CPU and 1.09% of memory, completing the analysis in just over 6 seconds.
Notes: Zeek is only the open-source tool used to evaluate intrusion detection in agricultural IoT; the study does not examine OSS project lifecycle or abandonment-related concerns.

Author: G. Smith; H. A. Ofe; J. Sandberg
Title: Digital Service Innovation from Open Data: Exploring the Value Proposition of an Open Data Marketplace
Abstract Note: Open data marketplaces have emerged as a mode of addressing open data adoption barriers. However, knowledge of how such marketplaces affect digital service innovation in open data ecosystems is limited. This paper explores their value proposition for open data users based on an exploratory case study. Five prominent perceived values are identified: lower task complexity, higher access to knowledge, increased possibilities to influence, lower risk and higher visibility. The impact on open data adoption barriers is analyzed and the consequences for ecosystem sustainability is discussed. The paper concludes that open data marketplaces can lower the threshold of using open data by providing better access to open data and associated support services, and by increasing knowledge transfer within the ecosystem.
Notes: The study examines open data marketplaces, adoption, and open-data ecosystem sustainability—not OSS projects or software-engineering lifecycle concerns.

Author: P. Morsali; M. Ahmad; Y. Qin; A. Mallik
Title: Unified Co-Optimization of Converter Parameters and Switching Modulation for Enhanced ZVS in Low-Lm DC–AC DABs
Abstract Note: This paper presents the harmonic superposition based theoretical approach for analyzing the impact of low magnetizing inductance Lm in extending the zero voltage switching (ZVS) range in a dc-ac dual active bridge (DAB) converter. A comprehensive design optimization framework has been developed to obtain the optimal ratio of magnetizing inductance to power transfer inductance and the optimal transformer turns ratio. An exponential decay function accounting for the non linearity of Coss has been derived and utilized in formulating the ZVS inequality constraints which are used to establish a multi-variable, multi-constraint and a single objective optimization framework to acquire the optimized control variables which enhance the average number of ZVS legs while co-optimizing the efficiency profile. Furthermore, the control strategy is implemented using a Fourier based regression model, enabling high accuracy and faster real time execution. Finally, a GaN based 500W/100kHz low-Lm DAB hardware prototype is developed and evaluated against the single inductor (SI) DAB model to validate the analytical framework and its effectiveness in extending the ZVS range. The experimental results for low-Lm DAB demonstrate an efficiency improvement of 2.8% and 3.2% at 20% and 40% load respectively, due to extended ZVS range and a slight efficiency decrease of 0.3% at full load as compared to SI-DAB.
Notes: The study concerns a hardware prototype and optimization of a dc-ac power converter, not OSS projects or ecosystems.

Author: L. Chen; W. Cui; B. Li; B. Li
Title: Optimizing coflow completion times with utility max-min fairness
Abstract Note: In data parallel frameworks such as MapReduce and Spark, a coflow represents a set of network flows used to transfer intermediate data between successive computation stages for a job. The completion time of a job is then determined by the collective behavior of such a coflow, rather than any individual flow within, and influenced by the amount of network bandwidth allocated to it. Different jobs in a shared cluster have different degrees of sensitivity to their completion times, modeled by their respective utility functions. In this paper, we focus on the design and implementation of a new utility optimal scheduler across competing coflows, in order to provide differential treatment to coflows with different degrees of sensitivity, yet still satisfying max-min fairness across these coflows. Though this objective can be formulated as a lexicographical maximization problem, it is challenging to solve in practice due to its inherent multi-objective and discrete nature. To address this challenge, we first divide the problem into iterative steps of single-objective subproblems; and in each of these steps, we then perform a series of transformations to obtain an equivalent linear programming (LP) problem, which can be efficiently solved in practice. To demonstrate that our solutions are practically feasible, we have implemented it as a real-world coflow scheduler based on the Varys open-source framework to evaluate its effectiveness.
Notes: The study optimizes network coflow scheduling in data-parallel jobs; Varys is only the open-source framework used for implementation, with no OSS lifecycle or maintenance topic studied.

Author: C. Markarian; C. Fachkha; T. Ullah Khan; A. Panthakkan; H. M. Khalid
Title: Why Algorithms Need Temporal Fairness
Abstract Note: Automated decision-making systems are increasingly entrusted with life-defining decisions, yet prevailing fairness frameworks largely treat these systems as static, one-shot processes. This creates a critical gap: existing methods fail to capture how repeated decisions accumulate, allowing small disparities to evolve into lasting inequities. Fairness, however, is inherently temporal. A single loan denial can delay credit building for years, while repeated résumé rejections can systematically exclude qualified candidates. To address this limitation, a unified mathematical framework for temporal fairness is introduced, evaluating fairness not as a snapshot but as an evolving trajectory of opportunities and outcomes. The framework assesses whether individuals and groups progress at comparable rates or face persistent exclusion, revealing lock-out effects, widening opportunity gaps, and delays in access. Interpretable temporal metrics such as cumulative access, lock-out rate, and time-to-first-approval make long-term fairness measurable and auditable. Theoretical analysis and empirical validation demonstrate how feedback loops can either reinforce inequities or foster inclusion, and how short-term parity may conflict with long-term equity. By reframing fairness as a temporal property, this work provides both theoretical foundations and empirically grounded tools for developing decision systems that are transparent, adaptive, and sustainable in their equity commitments.
Notes: The study concerns automated decision-making systems and fairness outcomes, with no OSS project, repository, or ecosystem population.

Author: K. A. Achmad; L. E. Nugroho; A. Djunaedi; Widyawan
Title: Smart City for Development: Towards a Conceptual Framework
Abstract Note: The level of urbanization, which may impact on urban problems, could be resolved through city development supported by the advanced information technology to build the smart(er) city. However, generally, a smart city is still developed and implemented sporadically, it does not yet adopt a particular framework. Currently, there is a limited conceptual analysis and integrated template, as well as a limited framework based on the regulations issues in Indonesia. Therefore, it is considered necessary to develop a conceptual framework of the smart city for development. The study was conducted based on synthesized and aggregated literature review to build a new conceptual framework. The analysis of literature showed a complementary existing smart city framework, including city services (basic services, non-basic services, and optional services); city resources (suprastructure, infrastructure, and infostructure); city (enterprise) architecture; and city goals (livability, workability, and sustainability). This research contributes to wider insights of smart city reference model for both Indonesia and other developing countries.
Notes: The study develops a smart-city framework; its population and subject are city services, resources, and architecture, not OSS projects or ecosystems.

Author: D. Rovniagin; A. Wool
Title: The Geometric Efficient Matching Algorithm for Firewalls
Abstract Note: Since firewalls need to filter all the traffic crossing the network perimeter, they should be able to sustain a very high throughput, or risk becoming a bottleneck. Firewall packet matching can be viewed as a point location problem: Each packet (point) has five fields (dimensions), which need to be checked against every firewall rule in order to find the first matching rule. Thus, algorithms from computational geometry can be applied. In this paper, we consider a classical algorithm that we adapted to the firewall domain. We call the resulting algorithm “Geometric Efficient Matching” (GEM). The GEM algorithm enjoys a logarithmic matching time performance. However, the algorithm's theoretical worst-case space complexity is O(n4) for a rule-base with n rules. Because of this perceived high space complexity, GEM-like algorithms were rejected as impractical by earlier works. Contrary to this conclusion, this paper shows that GEM is actually an excellent choice. Based on statistics from real firewall rule-bases, we created a Perimeter rules model that generates random, but nonuniform, rule-bases. We evaluated GEM via extensive simulation using the Perimeter rules model. Our simulations show that on such rule-bases, GEM uses near-linear space, and only needs approximately 13 MB of space for rule-bases of 5,000 rules. Moreover, with use of additional space improving heuristics, we have been able to reduce the space requirement to 2-3 MB for 5,000 rules. But most importantly, we integrated GEM into the code of the Linux iptables open-source firewall, and tested it on real traffic loads. Our GEM-iptables implementation managed to filter over 30,000 packets-per-second on a standard PC, even with 10,000 rules. Therefore, we believe that GEM is an efficient and practical algorithm for firewall packet matching.
Notes: The study evaluates a firewall packet-matching algorithm implemented in an open-source firewall; it does not investigate the OSS project's lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: J. Hu; Z. Zhang; C. S. Leow; W. L. Goh; Y. Gao
Title: LearnAFE: Circuit-Algorithm Co-Design Framework for Learnable Audio Analog Front-End
Abstract Note: This paper presents a circuit-algorithm co-design framework for learnable analog front-end (AFE) in audio signal classification. Designing AFE and backend classifiers separately is a common practice but non-ideal, as shown in this paper. Instead, this paper proposes a joint optimization of the backend classifier with the AFE’s transfer function to achieve system-level optimum. More specifically, the transfer function parameters of an analog bandpass filter (BPF) bank are tuned in a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)-aware training loop for the classifier. Using a co-design loss function LBPF, this work shows superior optimization of both the filter bank and the classifier. Implemented in open-source SKY130 130nm CMOS process, the optimized design achieved 90.5%–94.2% accuracy for 10-keyword classification task across a wide range of input signal SNR from 5 dB to 20 dB, with only 22k classifier parameters. Compared to conventional approach, the proposed audio AFE achieves 8.7% and 12.9% reduction in power and capacitor area respectively.
Notes: The study concerns an analog audio front-end and classifier; SKY130 is an open-source process used for implementation, not an OSS project or ecosystem under study.

Author: G. Srikanth Reddy
Title: Optimizing PostgreSQL Performance under High Transaction Loads: A Predictive and Consistency-Driven Perspective
Abstract Note: An open-source, enterprise level relational database system - PostgreSQL, is commonly used in a range of data-intensive environments because of its robustness, ACID transaction standards and extensible feature set. However, performance degradation becomes a serious concern at high transaction rates due to lock contention, I/O bottleneck, and replication lag. In this paper, we present a hybrid optimization architecture that aims at enhancing the performance of the PostgreSQL through a twofold strategy: Predictive Load Management (PLM) and Consistency-Driven Configuration (CDC). The PLM module makes use of state-of-the-art machine learning models that use XGBoost and LSTM to predict workload patterns, and tune system parameters such as memory buffers, parallelism and planner costs to increase both throughput and reduce latency. At the same time, the CDC module dynamically adjusts a transaction isolation level, a lock management scheme, and a replication strategy between request and response to maintain the data consistency and to reduce the concurrency overhead. Experimental evaluation on a PostgreSQL 15.1 cluster through pgBench as well as real workloads indicates that the hybrid scheme increases average TPS by 81%, alleviates query l latency of over 50%, and mitigates deadlocks and replication lag by 89% and 68%, respectively. Furthermore, automated index advice and partition-aware query planning all do a lot for the performance of query execution. The proposed system converts PostgreSQL from a statically configured DB into a self-adjusting engine that reacts to varying load in real-time and, simultaneously, maintains the consistency in the stored data. Our approach has implications in high-concurrency environments like financial systems, e-commerce apps, and cloud-native apps where performance and consistency must be equally balanced. The code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Srikanthrgudi/Optimizing-PostgreSQL-Performance-under-High-Transaction-Loads
Notes: The study evaluates database performance and configuration optimization; it does not investigate PostgreSQL project continuity, maintenance, inactivity, or abandonment.

Author: M. Mendula; A. Bujari; L. Foschini; P. Bellavista
Title: A Data-Driven Digital Twin for Urban Activity Monitoring
Abstract Note: The increasing pace of sensing and communication technology rollout is paving the way for concrete deployments of smart city applications, enabling a data-driven modeling of processes and the environment. In particular, the Urban Facility Management (UFM) process is growing in importance, recognized to have a direct impact on the sustainability and the development of our cities. In [1] we presented a system's view of a Digital Twin solution for the UFM process. The solution relies on (near)real-time data to quantify the activity index in an area of interest, used as a basis for planning decisions. In this study, we focus on the predictive subsystem, tasked with computing near-to-mid term predictions of the activity index, equipping UFM operators with a flexible decision-support system. Without loss of generality, we present an analysis of the vehicular traffic component, part of the activity index, assessing the accuracy of different predictive schemes, discussing some operational implications.
Notes: The study concerns smart-city urban facility management and vehicular-traffic prediction, with no OSS project or ecosystem population.

Author: G. Gemmi; L. Cerdà-Alabern; L. Navarro; L. Maccari
Title: Toward Smart Community Networks
Abstract Note: The advent of IEEE 802.11 in the late 1990s spurred the development of new network paradigms. In particular, new technology enthusiasts saw the potential of WiFi to bring broadband Internet connections to under-provisioned areas, giving rise to networks deployed and maintained by their users. This paradigm led to non-profit decentralized structures that grow by the unplanned addition of heterogeneous network devices: community networks (CNs). There have been hundreds of CN deployments worldwide; some have disappeared, while others have blossomed into complex networks with thousands of nodes. The networking research community has been aware of CNs, and many works studied CNs in their various aspects: design (routing, scalability, security), deployment, measurements, services, and so on. We argue that emerging technologies will give a new impetus to CNs by transforming them into smart CNs. This article aims to lay out the technical features of future CNs and encourage the research community to tackle the stimulating research challenges they raise.
Notes: The study concerns community networks, not OSS projects, repositories, or ecosystems.

Author: Z. Guo
Title: Mapping above ground carbon storage and sequestration using the InVEST model: A case study of three counties in Kenya
Abstract Note: Numerous studies have been undertaken to understand shifts in ecological indicators over time, employing various valuation methods and comprehensive ecological health monitoring efforts. This study presents a cost-effective approach to evaluating carbon storage and sequestration in Kenya, utilizing crop type maps derived from remote sensing data and the InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Environmental Services and Tradeoffs) carbon model. By harnessing publicly available satellite data and open-source ecosystem models, our spatially explicit analysis addresses concerns regarding data scarcity, providing essential insights into carbon stock dynamics across diverse land use types. We employ a proximity-based scenario generator to project future scenarios, including the expansion of select crop types, offering valuable tools for assessing land use changes and their impacts on carbon stocks. Spatial-temporal assessments uncover the dynamic nature of carbon stocks in response to land use changes over time.
Notes: The study evaluates carbon storage and land-use scenarios; open-source models are only tools, with no OSS project lifecycle or maintenance topic.

Author: J. Ludwig; D. Cline
Title: Challenges in Explaining Source Code Quality Assessment
Abstract Note: Creating and maintaining high-quality source code is especially important for critical systems such as those made for aerospace and military domains as well as for software product lines where long-lived, reusable modules are intended to be shared by multiple systems. CBR-Insight is an open-source automated assessment tool that relies on data science and interface design to provide an objective and understandable measure of source code quality. CBR-Insight supports the ability of technical and non-technical decision makers to verify that a project's software implementation follows through on promises around developing and sustaining reliable and maintainable software while managing technical debt. The primary contribution of this work is an in-depth discussion on how source code quality assessment is communicated to the entire development team in CBR-Insight, spanning from non-technical decision makers overseeing the project to the software developers responsible for source code. Specific issues discussed include understandability of the explanations provided by the user interface along with transparency and trust in the underlying, technically complex, calculations and scoring algorithms.
Notes: The study presents communication and usability of an open-source code-quality assessment tool; it does not investigate OSS project lifecycle, abandonment, or software decay.

Author: R. Roy; T. Ahmed; A. Majumdar
Title: Advanced Waste Detection Leveraging YOLO for High-Precision Classification
Abstract Note: This study aims to investigate the impact of improper waste disposal, addressing a critical gap in the existing literature and providing a sustainable waste management solution incorporating Artificial Intelligence. The research seeks new insights into advanced garbage detection systems. An open source pre-existing annotated dataset consisting of 3501 training set of images, 348 validation set of images and 228 test set images of a single class from roboflow was used to train all the models on 12 different versions of YOLO (You only look once) and 2 different versions of Gelan Series. All models were trained on an NVIDIA A10g 24GB GPU for 50 epochs, applying data augmentation techniques like rotation, cropping, and blurring. Among all models, YOLOV9-c and YOLOV8m achieved the best performance. Additionally, a full-stack application was developed as a Proof Of Concept using Flutter for the front end and Django for the back end.
Notes: The study uses an open-source dataset and AI models to detect waste; it does not investigate OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: D. Phillips; P. Hosein
Title: Generating Personalized News Podcasts from Print Media for those On the Go and the Blind
Abstract Note: Print media continues to be more trusted by the public than online sources. Unfortunately many people have little time to read such media and would prefer audio versions while driving or exercising and generally while busy with other activities. This also holds true for the visually impaired. We introduce an automated, personalized solution for emerging markets. This system follows the current shift to digital media which allows for more personalized solutions. Many can benefit from these implementations as they seek alternative revenue sources due to the decline in the revenue sources from print media. This system leverages freely available locally hosted Large Language Models (LLMS) and Text-To-Speech (TTS) synthesis tools to provide an accessible and sustainable alternative to traditional media. We compare two methods, one using Google’s cloud-based NotebookLM for summarization and personalization and another entirely locally hosted solution using the LLaMA model and a quantized version of the Orpheus Text-To-Speech model. Our implementation allows for both GPU-Based solutions as well as CPU-only solutions thus reducing the need for external cloud-based systems. We show that the local pipeline also provides comparable performance to external proprietary systems. It produces a personalized experience for users while maintaining a similar level of clarity and relevance to the proprietary system. A dual-layer evaluation approach was conducted to evaluate the technical performance of the model while also evaluating the potential to monetize an Artificial Intelligence (AI) news podcasting solution. The results showed a demand for an ad-free, subscription-based model, allowing users to have more variety in how they consume news. The proposed solution underscores the transformative potential of open AI tools and technology when used in the media space.
Notes: The study evaluates a news-podcast system using open AI tools; it does not investigate OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: X. Xu; X. Lu; Y. Yan; M. Tian; J. Wang
Title: ConfuciusLM: Exploring Confucian Personalized Instruction for Primary Learners With Large Language Models
Abstract Note: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a transformative force in educational informatization, offering unprecedented capabilities to simulate teacher–student interactions and generate adaptive instructional resources. However, general-purpose LLMs often provide direct outcome-oriented responses that lack pedagogical sensitivity, while existing educational models frequently prioritize rigid logical inquiry (e.g., Socratic questioning) over the affective and cognitive needs of novice learners. Such limitations can induce learning anxiety and impede the development of student confidence, particularly at the primary education level. To bridge this gap, we propose ConfuciusLM, a specialized educational LLM fine-tuned on a novel instructional dialogue dataset grounded in Confucian pedagogical philosophy. ConfuciusLM embodies a learner-centered paradigm by implementing a heuristic reasoning framework that integrates cognitive guidance with affective support and motivational scaffolding. Through both automated metrics and human-centered pedagogical evaluations, we demonstrate that ConfuciusLM exhibits superior performance compared to open-source LLMs of similar parameter scales in fostering positive learning dispositions and maintaining instructional coherence. This study advances the field of LLM-empowered education by proposing a robust framework that integrates Eastern pedagogical principles with artificial-intelligence-driven instructional design, thereby informing the development of more inclusive, empathetic, and human-centered intelligent tutoring systems. Importantly, the proposed approach offers concrete pedagogical and design implications for primary education, supporting the creation of learning environments that are psychologically safe, conducive to the development of self-efficacy, and capable of sustaining learner engagement under appropriate teacher guidance.
Notes: The study evaluates an educational LLM for instructional outcomes; open-source LLMs are comparison systems, with no OSS project lifecycle or maintenance topic.

Author: S. A. Nisperos; Y. Urano
Title: SMS text messaging: A ubiquitous tool for cheaper medicine in the Philippines
Abstract Note: Access to essential drugs is a key element for sustaining good health but medicines have become inaccessible to many because of very high prices. Consumers have no access to information regarding cheaper drugs that are alternatives to more expensive proprietary drugs. This study aimed to promote access to such information through the use of Short Message Service (SMS) and improve price transparency by creating a small database containing keywords that will easily provide consumers with detailed information about cheaper and branded drugs. The methodology being used consists of three parts. The first part includes interviewing key informants to obtain the necessary information from technical people with backgrounds and opinions relevant to the study. The collected data was then consolidated to make the system realistic through correlation with both internet and library research. The second step is by using an integrated software and modem so that consumers can get access to the database, allowing consumers to know the relative drug prices of different versions of the same drug simply by sending the name of the medicine anytime, anywhere. Lastly, a survey questionnaire was distributed to obtain immediate feedback regarding the system, including its ease or difficulty of use, applicability to actual needs, and problems that may arise. Moreover, this drug related information can be obtained even without an internet connection. This message handling system can save a lot of time and money to both consumers and patients and empower them to make informed decision-making on drug purchases.
Notes: The study evaluates an SMS system for medicine price information; OSS project lifecycle or abandonment is not its subject.

Author: R. Kandadi; S. Nimmala; R. Salakapuri
Title: SmartLeaf-ViT: Deep Vision Transformer Approach for Tomato Leaf Curl Virus Classification
Abstract Note: The Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (ToLCV) is a destructive viral affliction impacting tomato cultivation throughout India, particularly in semi-urban agricultural areas such as Karimguda near Ghatkesar, Hyderabad. Early identification is crucial to minimizing yield loss and enabling farmers to take prompt action. Conventional disease identification techniques are laborious and frequently inadequate in detecting early-stage illnesses. We propose an early categorization and control advice system for ToLCV utilizing Vision Transformers (ViT) combined with a domain-specific expert rule-based inference engine. The method utilizes a curated dataset comprising tomato leaf photos sourced from open-source platforms, such as PlantVillage, and field-level data collected from Karimguda farms. The ViT model was trained to categorize leaf pictures as either healthy or infected with ToLCV. Our model attained an accuracy of 93.8%, surpassing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)-based benchmarks, including ResNet50 (89.4%) and EfficientNet-B0 (90.7%). The categorization result is integrated with a rule-based engine to suggest suitable pesticide treatments according to disease severity, crop development stage, and regional climate circumstances. This framework offers farmers an advanced mobile-based early warning and advice system, facilitating precision agriculture and sustainable disease management.
Notes: Open-source platforms are only a source of tomato-leaf images; the study concerns plant disease classification and agricultural advice, not OSS lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: Z. Yang; Z. Khan; Y. Shen; H. Liu
Title: An Efficient Embedded Vision Framework for Real-Time Grapes Vineyard Unhealthy Leaves Detection and Precision Guided Spraying
Abstract Note: Precision spraying in vineyards demands accurate and efficient plant disease detection to minimize chemical waste and environmental contamination. This paper introduces DEPA-VINE, an improved lightweight YOLOv10-based detection framework designed for real-time grapevine leaf disease detection and autonomous spraying control. The network replaces the standard YOLOv10 backbone layers with stacked Mobile Inverted Bottleneck Convolution (MBConv) blocks and introduces a Dynamic Convolutional Aggregation (DCA) module at the input stage to enhance low-level feature extraction under motion blur and occlusion. The backbone concludes with a Spatial Pyramid Pooling and Multi-scale Enhanced Fusion (SPPMEF) block to strengthen global context modeling, while the head integrates a C2f-Extended LSK-enhanced Transformer (C2f-XLT) for improved semantic alignment and cross-scale feature fusion. The model is further optimized using the AdaBelief optimizer, which stabilizes convergence and improves generalization in lightweight settings. The proposed framework achieves 83.4% precision, a 66.8% F1-score, and 70.2% mAP@0.5 with only 6.1 GFLOPs, running at an average inference speed of 63.7 FPS on the Rockchip RK3588 embedded platform. Comparative evaluations against YOLOv5n, YOLOv7t, YOLOv6n, YOLOv12n, RetinaNet, and ATSS confirm superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and robustness in challenging vineyard conditions. Field experiments using an autonomous robotic sprayer demonstrate a 27% increase in droplet coverage on diseased foliage and a 90% reduction in unintended spraying on healthy leaves, leading to substantial pesticide savings. These results confirm the practicality of the proposed framework for real-time selective pesticide application, enabling more sustainable and automated vineyard management. The implementation code and dataset will be publicly available. Note to Practitioners—The proposed YOLOv10-based lightweight detection framework is designed for real-time deployment on embedded platforms such as the Rockchip RK3588, making it suitable for autonomous vineyard robots operating under resource-constrained conditions. Practitioners intending to adopt this approach should ensure proper dataset collection and annotation that reflects the target vineyard’s lighting conditions, occlusion patterns, and disease variability to achieve optimal generalization. The model’s low computational cost allows deployment on edge devices; however care must be taken to calibrate camera parameters and ensure stable network latency between the vision module and the actuator control unit for real-time spraying decisions. For robotic spraying systems, nozzle alignment and PWM duty-cycle mapping should be tuned based on field trials to balance droplet size, spray coverage, and chemical savings. The open-source implementation provided can serve as a baseline for further customization, such as adapting to other crops or integrating it with multi-robot coordination frameworks.
Notes: The study develops and evaluates a grapevine disease-detection and spraying system; open-source code is only an implementation resource, with no OSS lifecycle or maintenance topic.

Author: D. Beyer; A. E. Hassan
Title: Animated Visualization of Software History using Evolution Storyboards
Abstract Note: The understanding of the structure of a software system can be improved by analyzing the system's evolution during development. Visualizations of software history that provide only static views do not capture the dynamic nature of software evolution. We present a new visualization technique, the Evolution Storyboard, which provides dynamic views of the evolution of a software's structure. An evolution storyboard consists of a sequence of animated panels, which highlight the structural changes in the system; one panel for each considered time period. Using storyboards, engineers can spot good design, signs of structural decay, or the spread of cross cutting concerns in the code. We implemented our concepts in a tool, which automatically extracts software dependency graphs from version control repositories and computes storyboards based on panels for different time periods. For applying our approach in practice, we provide a step by step guide that others can follow along the storyboard visualizations, in order to study the evolution of large systems. We have applied our method to several large open source software systems. In this paper, we demonstrate that our method provides additional information (compared to static views) on the ArgoUML project, an open source UML modeling tool

Author: G. Mishra; U. Mamodiya; A. Avasthi
Title: Software Automated Model Lifecycle Management
Abstract Note: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence into enterprise and industrial environments has heightened the operational complexity of maintaining machine learning (ML) models in production. Automated Model Lifecycle Management (AMLM) provides a unified and systematic approach to standardizing model operations across all lifecycle phases—ranging from data versioning and experimentation to deployment, continuous monitoring, and governance. Traditional manual workflows often introduce versioning conflicts, reproducibility issues, and delayed responses to model degradation. AMLM mitigates these challenges through a fully automated and auditable pipeline that combines continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD), experiment tracking, model packaging, automated drift detection, and governed model updates within a single framework.The proposed AMLM architecture integrates open-source ecosystems such as MLflow for model registry and TFX/Kubeflow-inspired pipelines for orchestrating production workflows. Central to the system is a modular policy engine that governs promotion, rollback, and retraining decisions while ensuring adherence to fairness, performance, and privacy constraints. A reproducible evaluation setup and a benchmark experiment under synthetic data drift scenarios demonstrate measurable improvements in operational resilience, deployment latency, and recovery efficiency.Beyond technical automation, AMLM fosters transparency, accountability, and compliance by embedding governance checkpoints and privacy-preserving mechanisms throughout the workflow. The framework serves as a practical blueprint for organizations aiming to reduce time-to-production, minimize failure risks, and enhance the reliability of AI-enabled operations.
Notes: The study evaluates lifecycle management of production ML models; open-source tools are components of the framework, not OSS projects whose abandonment or maintenance is studied.

Author: Nurkhanifah; D. Athina; A. Afifah Rahmi; A. Ernesto; M. Erza Aminanto; B. Ilmi Nasution; N. Laily Romadhotul Husna; J. Intan Kanggrawan; Y. Nugraha
Title: Availability Investigation of Green Open Space and Slum Neighborhoods Areas to Flood Potential in Jakarta Using Geospatial Analysis
Abstract Note: The city of DKI Jakarta faces challenges of increasing population growth and migration. This phenomenon has led to a rising demand for land, driving land conversion and the development of densely populated residential areas, including slum areas. The impact threatens environmental sustainability, as the water infiltration areas experience a decrease and increase the risk of floods. This project calculates the suitability of green open space availability in Jakarta while analyzing the availability of green open spaces and slum environments regarding the flood potential in Jakarta using correlation and clustering analysis, thereby generating recommendations for areas based on the urgency of flood management. The initial stage involves exploratory data analysis to interpret the distribution of green open spaces (RTH), slum areas, and flood conditions based on secondary data. A quantitative descriptive approach with correlation research method is applied to explore the relationship between RTH, slum environments, and flood conditions. K-Means Clustering is used to identify patterns and classifications emerging from the data. The novelty introduced is the integration of correlation analysis with cluster analysis on geospatial data, where cluster analysis is conducted based on the results of the correlation analysis. The methods employed demonstrate a correlation between slum environmental conditions and flood potential in Jakarta. The combination of the results from the methods employed yields recommendations for intervention in the districts of Jatinegara and Cengkareng, which have a high urgency for addressing slum settlements due to their high correlation with floods.
Notes: The study population is Jakarta’s green spaces, slum neighborhoods, and flood conditions, not OSS projects or ecosystems.

Author: Y. H. Cho; W. H. Mangione-Smith
Title: Deep packet filter with dedicated logic and read only memories
Abstract Note: Searching for multiple string patterns in a stream of data is a computationally expensive task. The speed of the search pattern module determines the overall performance of deep packet inspection firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), and intrusion prevention systems (IPS). For example, one open source IDS configured for 845 patterns, can sustain a throughput of only 50 Mbps running on a dual 1-GHz Pentium III system. Using such systems would not be practical for filtering high speed networks with over 1 Gbps traffic. Some of these systems are implemented with field programmable gate arrays (FPGA) so that they are fast and programmable. However, such FPGA filters tend to be too large to be mapped on to a single FPGA. By sharing the common sublogic in the design, we can effectively shrink the footprint of the filter. Then, for a large subset of the patterns, the logic area can be further reduced by using a memory based architecture. These design methods allow our filter for 2064 attack patterns to map onto a single Xilinx Spartan 3-XC3S2000 FPGA with a filtering rate of over 3 Gbps of network traffic.
Notes: The study uses an open-source IDS as an example but focuses on FPGA-based packet-filter performance, not OSS project lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: L. Luthra; R. Agarwal; V. Sisaudia
Title: Cochleogram-Based Audio Forgery Detection Using CNN With Self-Attention and Squeeze-&-Excitation Layers (CAF-SE)
Abstract Note: The usage of free and open source tools, combined with advances in artificial intelligence, has significantly reduced the restrictions on generating fake or synthetic speech. This growing accessibility poses serious challenges to the field of audio forgery detection. As a result, ensuring the authenticity of audio content has become critical for protecting digital security and sustaining confidence in voice-based communication systems. This paper proposes Cochleogram-Based Audio Forgery Detection with Self-attention & Squeeze and Excitation (CAF-SE). CAFSE is a novel framework to classify real and fake audio using a convolutional neural network (CNN) enhanced by self-attention and squeeze-&-excitation (SE) layers. We introduce a robust training pipeline that incorporates $\mathbf{5}$-fold cross-validation, and performance is assessed using equal error rate (EER), accuracy, and F1 score. CAF-SE processes cochleograms, a time-frequency representation of audio signals, to capture subtle manipulations indicative of forgery. The model integrates multi-head selfattention to model global dependencies and SE to recalibrate channel-wise feature responses, improving classification accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate an accuracy of 0.9823, an $F 1$ score of 0.9830, and an EER of 0.0310 across folds in the release-in-the-wild (RITW) dataset and an accuracy of 0.9774, an F1 score of 0.9704, and an EER of 0.0191 across folds in real-fake audio datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in discriminating original from fake audio. Our findings suggest that SE-enhanced CNNs, combined with cochleogram augmentation, offer a promising solution for audio forgery detection.
Notes: The study evaluates an audio-forgery detection model; open-source tools are only mentioned as context, with no OSS project lifecycle topic.

Author: S. M. G; S. J; H. R
Title: Intelligent IoT-Driven Predictive Indoor Air Quality Management Framework for Educational Environments using Multi-Sensor Integration and Cloud-based Machine Learning Analytics
Abstract Note: The deterioration of the indoor air quality (IAQ) in schools is a major causative health problem and interferes with the efficiency of learning. The paper will describe an IoTbased IAQ management system based on the ESP32 to monitor in real-time, where the MQ2, MQ7, and MQ135 sensors are required to identify the presence of smoke, carbon monoxide, and dangerous gases. The sensor data is sent to a cloud solution where MATLAB is used to analyses the sensor data and machine learning models predict the trends of IAQ and preempt anomalies. The system makes automatic warning and suggestions to assure the best air quality, which allows effective prompt interventions. Complex analytics are used to detect patterns, correlations and source of pollutants enabling administrators to adopt specific action strategies. The experimental validation proves to be very accurate to detect pollutants and predict them. This open-source framework is scalable and provides real-time, intelligent decision support that can result into healthier school environments and provide the future basis of school IAQ optimization.
Notes: The study evaluates an open-source IAQ monitoring framework for school environments, not OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: Á. Oliveira; M. Campolargo
Title: From Smart Cities to Human Smart Cities
Abstract Note: This paper argues that current technology-driven implementations of Smart Cities, although being an important step in the right direction, fall short in exploiting the most important human dimension of cities. The paper argues therefore in support of the concept of Human Smart Cities. In a Human Smart City, people rather than technology are the true actors of the urban "smartness". The creation of a participatory innovation ecosystem in which citizens and communities interact with public authorities and knowledge developers is key. Such collaborative interaction leads to co-designed user centered innovation services and calls for new governance models. The urban transformation in which citizens are the main "drivers of change" through their empowerment and motivation ensures that the major city challenges can be addressed, including sustainable behavior transformations. Furthermore, the authors argue that the city challenges can be more effectively addressed at the scale of neighborhood and they provide examples and experiences that demonstrate the viability, importance and impact of such approach. The paper builds on the experience of implementing Human Smart Cities projects in 27 European cities located in 17 different countries. Details of the technologies, methodologies, tools and policies are illustrated with examples extracted from the project My Neighbourhood.
Notes: The study concerns smart-city projects and citizen participation, not OSS projects, repositories, or ecosystems.

Author: G. Ankatwar; C. Dhawale
Title: Enhancing Crop Disease Detection Systems With Explainable AI Techniques for Deep Learning Models Using Spectral Imaging
Abstract Note: Recognizing crop diseases at an early stage is essential for modern agriculture because it greatly enhances crop output and decreases economic losses. Manual examination and specialized expertise are the backbone of traditional disease detection approaches, but they can be exhausting and error-prone. In response to these difficulties, Deep Learning (DL) models have become an effective means of improving agricultural disease detection systems. Through autonomous learning and feature extraction from cropped images, these models-especially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have shown to be quite effective in image categorization tasks. Train deep-learning models to accurately identify a broad range of illnesses by using massive datasets of categorized crop images. Improved food security and more sustainable farming practices are the end results of incorporating DL models into crop disease identification systems, which secures and improves diagnosis while giving farmers more agency to make well-informed choices. As for crop disease prediction, we also tested the efficacy of several fine-tuning TL models such Efficient-Net, Squeeze-Net, and Dense-Net-121. Models were trained using the open-source Plant Village dataset. The study found that the Dense-net-121 model achieved the highest accuracy rates, with 98.5% on the training dataset and 97.85% on the testing dataset.
Notes: The study uses an open-source crop-image dataset to evaluate disease-detection models; it does not investigate OSS project lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: M. S. Sakib; X. Wang
Title: PyPSA-Based Analysis of Power Systems with Integrated Renewable Energy Sources
Abstract Note: The increasing integration of renewable energy sources (RES), particularly solar and wind, presents both significant opportunities and operational challenges for modern power systems. While these sources contribute to reduced carbon emissions and advance sustainability objectives, their intermittent nature can affect grid stability and efficiency. This study investigates the impact of solar photovoltaic (PV) integration on the IEEE 14-bus test system using Python for Power System Analysis (PyPSA), an open-source tool for energy system modeling and optimization. Solar PV generators were implemented at buses 9 and 14, and a 24 -hour time-series simulation was conducted using real irradiance data. The analysis emphasizes voltage stability, rotor angle deviation, generator dispatch, and transmission line loading. The results indicate that the system maintains stability under moderate levels of solar penetration, with bus voltages and line flows remaining within acceptable operational limits. Although reverse power flow occurs during peak solar generation hours, it does not adversely impact overall system reliability. These findings support the technical feasibility of integrating distributed solar PV into conventional power system infrastructure.
Notes: Open-source software is only the modeling tool; the study analyzes power-system stability under solar integration, not OSS lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: M. Kluge; R. A. Avalos-Zúñiga
Title: Aerodynamic Analysis of Bluff Bodies for VortexInduced Vibration Energy Harvesting
Abstract Note: The global change toward sustainable energy solutions has increased interest in energy harvesting from fluid flows, particularly through vortex-induced vibrations (VIV). This study explores a VIV-based energy generation system, leveraging transverse oscillations of bluff bodies to convert kinetic energy into electricity. A computational framework was developed to analyze the aerodynamic efficiency of two-dimensional geometries, focusing on the lift-to-drag ratio (LDR) as a key performance metric. A Python-based numerical routine was implemented using open-source tools (Gmsh for meshing, Elmer FEM for simulation) to evaluate LDR for various geometries, validated against benchmark data. Key findings reveal that a rhombus cross-section outperforms circular and elliptical shapes, achieving a $\mathbf{5 1 \%}$ higher LDR. Modifications like corner truncation and edge curvature further enhanced efficiency by up to $1.5 \%$ and $45 \%$, respectively. The study underlines the importance of geometric optimization for VIV energy harvesters, demonstrating that tailored bluff-body designs can significantly improve energy conversion. This work contributes to the advancement of renewable energy technologies by providing a computational tool for systematic geometry evaluation and identifying optimal shapes for VIV-based systems. Future research should explore 3D simulations, dynamic fluid-structure interactions, and experimental validation to bond theoretical insights with practical applications.
Notes: Open-source tools are only used to analyze energy-harvester geometries; the study does not examine OSS project lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: S. Raza; P. Misra; Z. He; T. Voigt
Title: Bluetooth smart: An enabling technology for the Internet of Things
Abstract Note: The past couple of years have seen a heightened interest in the Internet of Things (IoT), transcending industry, academia and government. As with new ideas that hold immense potential, the optimism of IoT has also exaggerated the underlying technologies well before they can mature into a sustainable ecosystem. While 6LoWPAN has emerged as a disruptive technology that brings IP capability to networks of resource constrained devices, a suitable radio technology for this device class is still debatable. In the recent past, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) — a subset of the Bluetooth v4.0 stack — has surfaced as an appealing alternative that provides a low-power and loosely coupled mechanism for sensor data collection with ubiquitous units (e.g., smartphones and tablets). When Bluetooth 4.0 was first released, it was not targeted for IP-connected devices but for communication between two neighboring peers. However, the latest release of Bluetooth 4.2 offers features that makes Bluetooth LE a competitive candidate among the available low-power communication technologies in the IoT space. In this paper, we discuss the novel features of Bluetooth LE and its applicability in 6LoWPAN networks. We also highlight important research questions and pointers for potential improvement for its greater impact.
Notes: The study concerns Bluetooth LE and 6LoWPAN technologies for IoT, not OSS projects, repositories, or ecosystems.

Author: M. Thankappan; N. K. Nataraj; D. K S; A. Jayaraj; A. Joby; A. Asokan
Title: AI-Enabled Robotic Surveillance System for Critical Infrastructure
Abstract Note: Traditional monitoring approaches often experience blind spots and high resource utilization at such a crucial time of security. In our study, we design a small-scaled autonomous vehicle model with smart sensors that is to be equipped with an AI model in a Raspberry Pi for effective and reliable self-sustained monitoring of critical infrastructure to overcome the problems. The core AI model was specifically designed to detect in real-time anomalies such as a fire, a fight, vandalism, explosion, etc. The AI model is a modified version of an open source repository available on github named “Real-world Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Videos (pytorch) [11]”. This technology ensures speedy response time by stopping the vehicle, starting video recording, and forwarding the real-time footage to security personnel upon detecting an anomaly. This innovative solution allows for mobilization and cost-effectiveness, improving surveillance coverage, and diminished dependence on constant human oversight. Exploiting advances in artificial intelligence and robotics, the project delivers a scalable real-time monitoring system deployable into a wide range of critical infrastructure environments. This initiative represents practical application of AI towards improving public safety and building a stronger security posture in facilities that house critical infrastructure.
Notes: OSS is only the source of a modified AI model; the study evaluates a robotic surveillance system, not OSS project lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: F. Naguji; N. Kumar Jadav; S. Tanwar; G. Pau; G. Sharma; F. Alqahtani; A. Tolba
Title: GreenLand: A Secure Land Registration Scheme for Blockchain and AI-Enabled Agriculture Industry 5.0
Abstract Note: The main aim of the proposed system is to facilitate secure and protected land registry in the domain of agriculture Industry 5.0. Considering the outlook of issues associated with it, we considered the blockchain and AI-based technology to fulfill the purpose of secure land registry. Establishing and confirming land ownership is essential for the land registry system in ensuring the protection of ownership rights, particularly crucial in the contexts of agriculture and Industry 5.0. In these sectors, land serves as a crucial resource for sustainable development and industrial innovation. Most of the existing works rely on legacy and centralized system to store land records; which result in high incidences of forgery and fraud. Therefore, maintaining a robust land registry system is essential to fostering economic investments, promoting green practices, and facilitating equitable access to land resources in agriculture and Industry 5.0 ecosystem. We proposed an AI and blockchain-enabled land registry system for agriculture and industry 5.0 that offers a more reliable, transparent, and efficient solution to the challenges of lack of transparency, data tampering, and inefficiency, which can result in disputes, fraudulent claims, and a lack of trust during the land registry. AI models, such as logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and light gradient boosting machine (LGBM), are employed to classify the fraud and non-fraud land data. Only the non-fraud land data is forwarded into the blockchain network, thereby reducing the computational overhead of the proposed land registry system. In the blockchain network, we designed various smart contracts that validate the land data with unparalleled efficiency and security. Further, the slither solidity source analyzer tool is used for smart contract vulnerability assessment. After the assessment, the smart contract is deployed using the Sepolia test network. The non-fraudulent land data is redirected to the interplanetary file system (IPFS) that stores the original data and forwards the associated hash into the blockchain’s immutable ledger. The entire proposed system is evaluated with different performance parameters, such as AI statistical measures including accuracy, ROC, log-loss score, blockchain scalability comparison, gas cost utilization, and bandwidth utilization. Furthermore, the vulnerability assessment of the smart contract is analyzed using Slither to highlight the working of proposed system without any vulnerabilities. The proposed blockchain and AI-based land registry system ensure a secure and intelligent pipeline to combat against land forgery activities.
Notes: The study proposes and evaluates a blockchain/AI land-registry system; OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment is not investigated.

Author: B. K. S. G; S. Danush; S. A. Rao; B. R. Shambhavi
Title: Fine-Tuning F5-TTS for Indian English Speech Synthesis
Abstract Note: Artificial intelligence is transforming synthetic speech, making it possible to generate digital voices that sound remarkably real. While recent advances in text-to-speech technology have produced natural and expressive audio, creating voices that genuinely capture the character of Indian English remains a major challenge. In this work, we fine-tuned a leading TTS model using open source datasets designed to represent the diversity of Indian English. Our process included careful data selection, thorough cleaning, and modern training techniques for improved realism. We evaluated our system using both technical metrics and feedback from human listeners. The results showed clear gains over previous models, with synthesized voices that felt more genuine and relatable for Indian English speakers. Our evaluation combined objective measures of intelligibility and acoustic quality with perceptual ratings, offering a comprehensive assessment strategy for future speech synthesis systems targeting diverse linguistic communities.
Notes: The study evaluates a speech-synthesis model using open-source datasets; it does not examine OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: D. Miorandi; I. Carreras; E. Gregori; I. Graham; J. Stewart
Title: Measuring net neutrality in mobile Internet: Towards a crowdsensing-based citizen observatory
Abstract Note: Smartphones and tablets are becoming the de facto standard devices for accessing Internet content and services. The debate on net neutrality, recognised as a key techno-social component of Internet governance, has focused so far on “wired” Internet. In this position paper we advocate the use of a crowdsensing approach, coupled with Open Data philosophy, as the way to build a “citizen observatory” on net neutrality in mobile Internet. This is expected to positively impact the evolution towards a sustainable mobile Internet governance.
Notes: The position paper concerns mobile Internet governance and net neutrality; OSS is not the study population, and it does not investigate OSS lifecycle or abandonment-related concepts.

Author: S. P. Azad; B. Niazmand; P. Ellervee; J. Raik; G. Jervan; T. Hollstein
Title: SoCDep2: A framework for dependable task deployment on many-core systems under mixed-criticality constraints
Abstract Note: In this paper, an open-source framework for task deployment of mixed-critical and non-critical applications under dependability constraints in Network-on-Chip (NoC) based systems is introduced. This system level design space exploration is guided by a System Health Monitoring Unit which keeps a holistic view of system health status. The framework supports task clustering, mapping and scheduling of different applications, using different heuristics, on a NoC-based architecture which can have different topologies. This enables exploration of 2D and 3D typologies, any turn model based routing algorithm, fault monitoring mechanisms and different fault models (Link, Turn, Node).
Notes: The study introduces an open-source framework for task deployment and system-level design exploration; it does not investigate OSS project lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: P. Sivaraman; G. Prabaharan; V. Rajasekar; V. Sarveshwaran
Title: Efficient Auto Scaling of Pods in Kubernetes: Accelerating Continuous Delivery with KEPTN
Abstract Note: Model deployment in machine learning has become recognised as an emerging field of research in recent years. It can be viewed as a method similar to conventional software development. Organisations can move more quickly and smoothly when development and operations (DevOps) practises like Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) are used. Various software development approaches are available for enterprise applications. Micro-services architecture has become very popular among these accessible software development approaches. Enterprise applications, which are frequently sophisticated and require out-of-the-box scalability and low latency, integrate well with the micro-service design. For enterprise applications, microservices in a containerized cloud environment are particularly helpful. It is also extremely important from a software development standpoint in the software business to find and fix errors early on in the development process rather than once they have reached the level of the production environment. Kubernetes is a creative and well-integrated platform solution for running and controlling containerized applications gracefully and effectively. Developers can easily build and maintain clusters with the managed Kubernetes service known as AKS. It makes containerized application deployment and management possible. AKS offers serverless Kubernetes, a continuous integration and delivery experience that is integrated, as well as enterprise-level security and governance. Users of Microsoft Azure will find that AKS offers several appealing features that make it simple to set up, administer, scale, and monitor an AKS cluster.
Notes: The record concerns Kubernetes autoscaling and CI/CD deployment practices, not OSS project abandonment, maintenance, or lifecycle-related outcomes.

Author: R. Rosati; F. Antonini; N. Muralikrishna; F. Tonetto; A. Mancini
Title: Improving Industrial Question Answering Chatbots with Domain-Specific LLMs Fine-Tuning
Abstract Note: The industrial landscape is experiencing a significant transformation and there is a growing emphasis on human-machine collaboration, personalization, and sustainable manufacturing. Within this context, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as pivotal Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools that enhance communication, streamline operations, and support complex decision-making tasks through advanced natural language processing capabilities. This paper explores the process of fine-tuning a foundational general-purpose LLM, specifically the open-source LLaMA 3 model, to cater to industrial applications. We delve into the methodology of fine-tuning LLaMA on domain-specific data from two distinct industrial scenarios (i.e., product management and production line operations). Our results demonstrate significant improvements in the model’s performance, accuracy, and relevance in generating responses, thereby enhancing decision-making and operational processes in industrial settings. Additionally, we propose the integration of the fine-tuned model into a chatbot system designed to assist human operators by providing targeted, accurate responses in real-time. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive guide for industry practitioners and researchers to harness the power of LLMs for specialized industrial tasks, ultimately contributing to the advancement of intelligent industrial automation and decision-making systems.
Notes: The study fine-tunes an open-source LLM for industrial chatbot applications; it does not examine the model’s or an OSS project’s maintenance, continuity, or lifecycle.

Author: A. Gupta; S. Gupta; A. Shukla
Title: Real-Time Digital Simulation for Investigating Transient Stability of Power System Network
Abstract Note: This paper examines the power swing explicitly before and after a fault, which plays a crucial role in stabilizing the power system network during transient conditions. It analyzes the transient stability of the IEEE 5 bus network during a three-phase symmetrical fault occurrence and load variation. The purpose is to limit voltage transients during the fault by selecting appropriate Critical Clearing Time (CCT) and breaker resistance. Additionally, the article investigates the impact of wind generator integration on the voltage and frequency improvement of the power system network during load variations. The study employs a Real-Time Digital Simulator (RTDS) and an open-source software Power World Simulator (PWS). Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) are utilized to monitor the voltage and frequency of the network. The accuracy and effectiveness of the results obtained from the RTDS and PWS are compared to validate the power system transient stability analysis.
Notes: Open-source Power World Simulator is used as a tool; the study investigates power-system transient stability, not OSS project lifecycle or maintenance.

Author: M. A. Balaj; K. Oakley; M. Dobler; M. Winterburn; M. Hellwig; N. A. F. Lopes
Title: Preprocessing Pipelines for OT Network Traffic Capture Data in AI Cybersecurity Applications
Abstract Note: Digitalisation is driving a new level of focus on Cybersecurity in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Operationsal Technology (OT) environments. Various techniques to detect malicious activity in OT networks based on network traffic monitoring have been developed. These often use Aritficial Intelligence (AI), or rather Machine Learning (ML), algorithms to identify and classify the traffic as potentially malicious. Training and testing of these algorithms requires data in ML-processable formats; however, network traffic capture files are typically not ML-ready, i.e., they are usually not readily usable for the training of ML classifiers. This paper reviews the procedures for building current state-of-the-art OT network traffic datasets. By considering 17 different datasets, we discuss approaches used for dataset creation, attack simulation, and labelling, respectively. On this basis, this work proposes a new pipeline for processing PCAP files into ML-ready formats. The pipeline leverages currently available open source tools and includes a set of options to enable the pipeline to be tailored to specific ML/AI algorithms, OT protocols and attack types. While PCAP files can capture malicious traffic, there are no inherent labels present in PCAPs. Thus, a particular focus is on the different types of labelling strategies available for the pipeline. The pipeline provides a useful overview of the available network traffic data preprocessing options. It also supports a broader range of ML and cybersecurity practitioners when using raw network traffic datasets for ML learning purposes in OT environments. The practicability of the proposed pipeline is demonstrated by relabeling network traffic capture data of a publicly available PCAP dataset in two ways and by comparing the results to original labels.
Notes: The study develops and demonstrates an OT network-traffic preprocessing pipeline; open-source tools are used as implementation resources, with no OSS project lifecycle or abandonment topic.

Author: K. G. Crowther
Title: Risk-informed assessment of regional preparedness
Abstract Note: Risk-informed and sustainable preparedness of our nation's regions and localities is central to the safety and security of the United States. The first step to technology development for preparedness is clear requirements and correct methodologies. This paper presents methods for creating regional homeland security plans to ensure continuity of regional operations. First, regional preparedness strategy should focus on a region's vital socioeconomic interests. These industries can be identified through the application of key sector analysis methods that exploit large-scale and open-source databases reporting economic sector production and interdependence. Second, planning for regional preparedness should follow two complementary approaches focusing on catastrophic scenario-driven planning as well as all-hazards capabilities. Third, regional preparedness strategy should exploit existing organizations and preparedness governance structure. Most existing regional preparedness institutions organize around the concept of emergency support functions (ESFs). Defining the relationships between ESFs and critical infrastructure sectors will enable these existing organizations to broaden their mission to adopt more holistic preparedness planning and homeland security practices, and provide a foundation technology. This paper provides preliminary results from case studies in Virginia to illustrate each of these methods.
Notes: The study concerns regional homeland-security preparedness planning; open-source databases are only a data source, with no OSS project lifecycle or maintenance topic.

Author: F. J. Valente; L. P. Mendes
Title: The Right of Transparency for Citizens in the Context of GDPR Using Blockchain: A Proposed Architecture
Abstract Note: Amid intense contemporary debates over the need for greater control over personal data, the Brazilian State legislates on the subject and gives rise to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Taking advantage of this debate to ensure transparency - a fundamental right provided in the Federal Constitution and regulated through the Access to Information Act (ATIA), we have investigated the use of blockchain to maintain traceability of queries carried out by public entities to citizens' data. More specifically, we propose a blockchain-based system platform for querying a citizen's data and storing the trace of queries in the blockchain. The generated history can then be consulted by the citizen, obtaining the name of the organization that carried out the search and what data was searched. To demonstrate the technical and operational feasibility of the proposal, we have implemented a web/blockchain-based system and carried out functional and performance tests, including overhead comparisons with the introduction of blockchain registration. The results were analysed and discussed in the work.
Notes: The study proposes and tests a blockchain system for public entities to trace access to citizens’ data; it does not study OSS projects or ecosystems.

Author: S. Lochschmidt; S. Engels; R. Wille
Title: Towards Optimal Train Routing Using Microscopic Simulation on Moving Block Controlled Networks
Abstract Note: The demand for sustainable railway transportation is increasing over time. At the same time, the capacity of railway networks is limited. Hence, efficient algorithms for generating optimal timetables are of great interest. Previous research focuses on trains being separated by classical fixed block signaling systems. With modern control systems based on moving block, e.g., within the European Train Control System (ETCS), the principles of safely separating trains change significantly. Only limited research on optimal routing on such modern railway networks exists. With this work, we propose a simulation approach tailored to be used with heuristic optimization algorithms to tackle this problem. Moreover, we show how such a framework can allow for more general inputs to jointly optimize what is usually planned sequentially as of today. The simulation framework is included within the open-source Munich Train Control Toolkit (MTCT) available on GitHub at https://github.com/cda-tum/mtct.
Notes: The study develops a simulation framework for railway routing and timetabling; the open-source toolkit is an implementation, with no investigation of its lifecycle, maintenance, or abandonment.

Author: E.Poongodi; R. Mukdhar; N. G; S. S; Y. A
Title: A Hybrid SOM–NSGA-II Optimized Neural–Forest Framework for Accurate Air Quality Prognosis
Abstract Note: Rapid industrialization and urban expansion have significantly deteriorated air quality, posing serious risks to human health and environmental sustainability. Accurate air quality prediction is therefore essential for effective environmental monitoring and policy planning. This paper proposes a hybrid air quality prognosis framework that integrates Self-Organizing Map (SOM) clustering, NSGA-II based neural network optimization, and Random Forest classification. Historical air quality data obtained from the Kaggle open-source repository are first preprocessed using adaptive noise-resilient techniques to extract informative features. SOM is employed to identify latent pollutant relationships, while NSGA-II optimizes the neural network parameters to achieve a balance between prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. In parallel, a Random Forest classifier predicts Air Quality Index (AQI) categories based on CPCB standards. The outputs from both models are combined to produce reliable air quality forecasts. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an average AQI prediction accuracy of 98.4% and classification accuracy of 98.9%, outperforming conventional regression, support vector regression, and standalone neural network models.
Notes: The study develops air-quality prediction models; the Kaggle open-source repository is only a data source, with no OSS lifecycle or abandonment-related subject.

Author: H. Liang; Z. Li; Q. Wang; Y. Guo; X. Tao; J. H. Zheng
Title: Analytical Globally Optimal Solution for Multiperiod Self-Scheduling of Energy Storage via Parametric Dynamic Programming
Abstract Note: With the proliferation of energy storage, the optimal self-scheduling (OSS) for energy storage is fundamental across various energy management domains. The OSS problem is typically formulated as a mixed integer linear program, the solution of which relies on commercial solvers in current practice and is computationally intensive to achieve global optimality, hindering efficient exploitation of energy storage. To address this challenge, we propose an efficient and robust analytical solution method to achieve global optimality for OSSs. In this work, the OSS is formulated as a parametric program of the initial state of charge, and a recursive analytical solution algorithm (ASA) is devised to explicitly derive the optimal solution expressions within critical regions based on a forward-and-backward framework. The comprehensive simulation results show that the proposed ASA is substantially more efficient than prevalent solvers and solution methods and that it empirically exhibits linear scaling performance with increasing time horizons.
Notes: The study concerns optimal self-scheduling of energy storage systems, not open-source software projects or ecosystems.

Author: K. Nandakumar; J. Sharma; S. R. Qadri; D. Panigrahy
Title: Orbit Safe: An Integrated System for Space Object Collision Risk Assessment
Abstract Note: This project focuses on developing a viable hybrid deep-learning system for NEO (Near Earth Object) monitoring and risk assessment, using TLE (Two-Line Element) data from open-source datasets such as NASA’s NEO Database and CelesTrak. The system’s performance will be assessed alongside other existing models using precision, accuracy, recall, validation loss, and F1 scores. Our proposed model aims to drastically reduce the danger posed by natural NEOs, such as asteroids orbiting the Earth, as well as artificial NEOs, such as space debris. These objects pose a significant risk given the exponential rise in humanity’s spacefaring activities, as well as the rapid rise in space debris caused as a consequence of the Kessler Syndrome effect. If this issue is left unaddressed, it will inevitably lead to catastrophic results. Our proposed model will not only enhance NEO monitoring and risk assessment, but it will also help ensure the essential goal of achieving sustainability in space, in alignment with the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines set forth by UN COPUOS (Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space).
Notes: The study develops a space-object risk-assessment system using open-source datasets; its population and research subject are not OSS projects or ecosystems.

Author: E. Harika; J. Balaraju
Title: Next-Generation Cryptographic Approaches for Cloud Data Security: A Comprehensive Review of Techniques and Innovations
Abstract Note: The recent digital-era, data is a crucial resource for undertaking a diverse issue in government agencies, commercial enterprises and private organizations. Many open-source and commercial tools like Hadoop, HDP and CDH have configured to store, process and reuse data over longer periods of time because of its incremental growth. To enable data storage, processing and analysis both the private and public cloud platforms are frequently deployed in master-slave architectures. But some key risks such as loss of direct control, supply chain vulnerabilities, compliance gaps and AI threats such significant vulnerabilities arise within cloud computing environments as they outsource security control to third party protocols. This paper surveys different cryptographic approaches and various security protocols exclusively focussing on data at rest. This research article recommends metadata protection as a substitute which cut the computational costs without negotiating data security. In order to do so lightweight DNA-based data hiding solution is proposed as an efficient and scalable one.
Notes: The paper reviews cryptographic approaches for cloud data security and proposes data hiding; it does not study OSS project lifecycle or abandonment-related concepts.

Author: Tanvi Chawla; Tamanna Gahlawat; TanyaShree Thakur
Title: A Big Data Analytics–Based Architecture for Smart Farming
Abstract Note:
Summary

Smart farming is an evolving term that refers to the management of farms with use of latest technologies such as artificial intelligence, drones, Internet of Things (IoT), and robotics. The use of these modern techniques helps in increasing quality and quantity of products; at the same time, it optimizes the required human labor. The use of big data analytics in smart farming is discussed in this chapter. There is massive volume of data available that also has huge variety and is termed as big data. After capturing this data, we can analyze it and use it further for decision making. Big data is being used to provide a deep and predictive understanding of the farming operations. It is also used for driving operational decisions in real time and redesigning business processes for creating groundbreaking business models. The farmers at all levels are using information that is available on the internet, so, nowadays, the farming is becoming digitalized. With the advent of computer and machine learning, the irrigation sector has now become full of advanced sensors and tools. In smart farming, the devices are connected to soil and crop for collecting information and transmitting it to the farmer. On basis of this information, the farmer sees how much water or other things are required by the soil for the crop to grow.
